highlights.title: I Did Push-Ups With Snap’s Chunky AR Glasses
highlights.summary: They fit better than they look and stay put when you move, but Snap’s $2,195 Specs still feel like a developer prototype in search of a purpose.
body: I hadn’t expected to be doing augmented reality push-ups in the middle of the mall. Yet there I was, wearing bulky Snap Specs while facing the ground.

The Lens (what Snap calls apps on its augmented reality headset ) is called Thirty Ups. It is in Halloween mode now, so when I look down, a virtual cartoon Jack-o’-lantern sits right next to where I’m supposed to start working out. I’m not trying to get jacked right now, but my goal is to see if these gigantic smart glasses will fall off when I’m staring straight down and moving up and down.

I get into position and start my workout. When I go down and back up, a little virtual circle on the ground below me starts counting up. I don’t get to 30 push-ups. I’m surrounded by people, many of whom are now staring at me, and it feels too hot outside to keep going without feeling gross. I get in 12 reps before giving up. The glasses only count 11 because it tells me I “skipped” one. Great.
The nearby Snap representative is thrilled. “You’re the first person who’s tried that one,” he says. I’m also pleasantly surprised. These glasses seem huge, but they stayed on my face just fine.
points: They fit better than they look and stay put when you move, but Snap’s $2,195 Specs still feel like a developer prototype in search of a purpose.

highlights.title: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time
highlights.summary: This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test. They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about how they’d be graded.
body: AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, and the companies building and running them are mostly relying on luck and hindsight to mitigate any harmful impacts. They must do more to ensure safety. That’s why EU regulators and US agencies are rightfully calling for agent developers and deployers to monitor agents in real time. But these rules assume that companies can see what their agents are doing and why—when in reality, they lack sufficient visibility.

As agents roll out across critical sectors, from finance to government to medicine, we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent wide-ranging and potentially devastating consequences. And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires observability: the capacity to capture what the system did, process it into signals, and present those to humans or automated oversight systems. In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it. And as our recent research shows, current agent frameworks—the software that runs agents— do not reliably generate the crucial observability records we need to ensure that agents are deployed safely.

highlights.title: Aliens, Dinosaurs and a Father’s Death: ‘Kefi’ Director Saito Kisin Brings a Surreal Take on Grief to Tokyo
highlights.summary: Likely the strangest entry at this year’s Tokyo International Film Festival, the surreal “Kefi,” the debut feature by cinematographer Saito Kisin, mixes multiple short stories and multiple styles to make sense of the feelings around a complicated relationship with his late father.
body: “Initially, I wanted to do four series of short films and put it together, and that would become a feature,” Saito says. “And those four would all have individual themes. So the first one would be ethics. Second would be hypocrisy. There would be discrimination, and fourth would be life and death.”

The youngest of three brothers, Saito intended to loosely connect the project to his own family, with his shorts following three sisters instead. Then, in 2024, he received news that his father had died.

That news is echoed in the film’s opening. Shortly after a scene in which their absent father speaks about them in narration, an echo from beyond the grave, three sisters – oldest Kyo, middle child Asumi and youngest Kino – learn of his death. Like Saito’s own father, the girls’ father had been separated from the family since their parents’ divorce.
“To tell you the truth, when my father passed, I didn’t feel sad,” Saito says. “Well, the reason being my parents divorced about 10 years ago, I haven’t met him for about 10 or so years.”

highlights.title: The secret life of the scream park: fear, fainting, clowns – and ‘code brown’
highlights.summary: At Norfolk’s ‘premier scare attraction’ there are ghouls, chainsaws, satanic cults and a haunted hospital. But what goes on behind the scenes? ‘We always say to the scare actors, you’re going to think the boys will be the worst.
body: This is part of the workplace induction at PrimEvil, one of many immersive “scream parks” that pop up across the UK in the lead up to Halloween. For about £40 a ticket, groups of all ages spend the night roaming themed attractions and being terrorised by actors and special effects. Though the risks are minimal, the spikes in heart rate are very real.

For Francis and the rest of the team, PrimEvil is months in the making. The nightly production involves more than 100 actors and dozens of crew, spread across six themed attractions, each drawing from familiar horror tropes – the scary clowns at the Circus of Terror, the cannibalistic trailer-dwellers over at Route 666, the satanic cult of The Offering. The winding routes are designed to disorient you with strobe lights, smoke machines, mirrored walls, hidden doors, false exits and unstable floors. But it’s down to the performers to bring the nightmare to life.

highlights.title: Adam Mosseri says negativity around AI is ‘going to get worse’
highlights.summary: Asked about AI and the trend of college students booing tech CEOs at graduation ceremonies, Instagram head Adam Mosseri acknowledged in an interview that a lot of people really don't like AI, and it's not just young people and creatives.
body: The Instagram boss said that worries about AI come down to ‘a fear of being left behind in some way.’

It’s not only getting worse, it’s going to continue to get worse. I think we’re going to see more frustration and anger, some of it founded, some of it unfounded, over the next couple of years, and that’s going to make it hard for a lot of people, not just in the industry.

Mosseri claimed Instagram doesn’t rank AI creators differently, but raised the question of ranking quality, saying, “There’s a lot of great AI content out there, there’s also a lot of AI slop. Do we rank AI content as well as we rank non-AI content? Probably not.” Talking about AI slop again after previously bringing it up in a New Year’s slideshow dump, he said he thinks the term AI “slop” is used “too liberally.”

Instagram began cracking down on AI-generated profiles in August, after launching a label for AI accounts earlier this year, but misleading AI content like celebrity deepfakes remains an issue. Earlier this month, Mosseri said Instagram is “actively working out what to do” about AI fakes, but he noted, “I don’t think it’s practical for us to try and ban AI content from the platform.”

body: When Dyson announced it was entering the toothbrush market, the world responded almost as one: “Four hundred and twenty pounds? For a toothbrush!?”

No, it wasn’t a stray decimal point – or if it was, Dyson is doubling down and leaning into the mistake. Unlike high-end brushes from Oral-B or Philips Sonicare, where the “recommended” in “recommended retail price” is doing a heroic amount of heavy lifting given the frequent discounts, the Dyson CameraJet will actually set you back £419.99.

The CameraJet is an electric toothbrush and a water flosser, so if you were being charitable – or merely looking for a way to justify the cost to yourself – you could call this two for the price of one on the best electric toothbrushes and water flossers.

There’s a lot of clever technology here, and Dyson’s commitment to doing something different should be applauded, even if it’s just to give your hands something to do besides reaching for your credit card.

highlights.summary: Fatal Frame creator and director Makoto Shibata once said that the most frightening thing is people's imaginations, which are populated by monsters that we can't see. When designing the first installment of one of the 2000s' most iconic horror series, his desire was to create a game that would make…
body: As a kid who grew up with Resident Evil 3 Nemesis and Silent Hill as the epitome of horror games, I became fascinated and terrified by Fatal Frame. Released by Tecmo in 2001 in Japan for the PlayStation 2, the game was created by Shibata and Keisuki Kikuchi, who had worked together before on the Deception series. In Fatal Frame, we play as Miku Hinasaki, a young woman looking for her brother, who has disappeared in the haunted Himoru Mansion. To protect herself, she has only an old camera called Camera Obscura, which is capable of damaging and capturing spirits. While characters and settings change between titles, all games in the series follow a similar structure.

highlights.title: AI has come for Arizona’s water
highlights.summary: A hulking gray giant rises from the desert. Inside, engineers create the force behind our phones and computers and appliances, our streaming services and search engines and chatbots and vibe-coded apps and websites.
body: I stand before the savior of Arizona’s economy. Like all great deities, it demands sacrifice. In the desert, nothing is more precious than water, and water is what must be given — nearly 5 million gallons a day, every day, sourced from Phoenix’s municipal supply. The offering has been well worth it.

All of this is the fruit of the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, the world’s leading producer of microchips. Its Arizona operation is the result of a pre-pandemic gamble Phoenix made to revive its sluggish economy, which never quite rebounded from the Great Recession. Now TSMC’s foundry looms over the city’s outskirts.
Now the state has a sixth C, Arizona native Christine Mackay tells me. “Chips.”

highlights.title: Creating AI value with enterprise context
highlights.summary: Across a business, any number of AI platforms, systems, and tools may be at work simultaneously—for example, AI-powered customer platforms, conversational assistants, and workflow and process automation tools. Each one is sophisticated, advanced, and quick to respond.
body: An MIT Technology Review Insights poll finds that while every organization surveyed is using AI today to some degree, fewer than one in five (16%) are extracting transformative value from their deployments. The largest percentage of respondents (40%) say they are seeing moderate gains in specific tasks or teams, while 21% report meaningful gains, leaving 23% that are seeing minimal returns or none at all.

Companies are mostly still piloting AI use cases (according to 38% of respondents) or using it to assist employees’ work with tools like co-pilots or chat assistants (35%). Just 12% of enterprises have AI agents in production and 3% say they are using AI to do most of the work in key processes.

“There’s a big gap between what the models are capable of and how the models are actually being useful inside organizations,” says Prukalpa Sankar, co-founder of Atlan. “For every real-life intent and purpose, artificial general intelligence is already here. It’s just not really useful in most companies today.”

highlights.title: How Bayern Munich fell in love with Kane
highlights.summary: It was approaching midnight when Harry Kane emerged to take the congratulations of the media patiently waiting for a word with Bayern Munich's new Ballon d'Or winner. He had not even played in their 6-1 cup win over Magdeburg but it still felt like his night.
body: Harry Kane made a hero's return to the Allianz Arena for Bayern Munich's game against Magdeburg and was saluted by his teammates and fans. With insight from the legendary Lothar Matthaus, Adam Bate reports from Munich on Kane's Bayern romance...

He joked about his children playing with the trophy. He responded to calls for him to be knighted: "I would feel weird if everyone called me Sir." Bizarrely, he even faced questions about being given a golden schnitzel: "I saw that one more as a trophy than to eat it."

Kane insists that he was ready to play but it is clear that what he refers to himself as "a big emotional load" has had an impact on him. "It feels like the Freiburg game was six weeks ago," he said. In reality, it was Sunday. "So much has happened in the last 48 hours."

Naturally, much of the focus since has been on him becoming only the fifth Englishman to claim this award and the first in a quarter of a century. But Bayern have waited two decades longer than that to see one of their own claim this prize. They adore Kane.

highlights.title: I Gave My Blood to the AI Death Clock
highlights.summary: Death Clock promises to predict when you’re going to die and help you extend your time on Earth. After a month, I felt like it was sucking the life out of me.
body: So says my iPhone screen, where Death Clock, an AI -powered longevity app that predicts life expectancy based on your medical habits and lifestyle, has produced an image of a smiling grim reaper to celebrate my expiration date. There he was one September morning, looking especially thrilled about the reveal, gesturing with a peace sign as he reclined in a doughnut-shaped pool inflatable under that giant number: 74.

I have never resented getting older, but I suppose that’s younger than I’d like to be when my time is up. In the last four years—years that brought the passing of my grandmother and aunt within 18 months—I’ve become hyperaware of how finite my days are. Since turning 40 in January, I’ve also experienced daily reminders of aging: inexplicable pains that rotate between my back, neck, and hips. Spiritually, I feel young; physically, my body screams otherwise. Aging is natural, but I had a creeping suspicion I could buy myself more time.

In-form Chesterfield winger Markanday is a proud British-Indian, who last week celebrated five years since becoming the first British South Asian to play for Tottenham Hotspur in 140 years of the club's history.

highlights.title: ‘Looming stone towers like Maya temples’: a hike through Snowdonia’s slate country
highlights.summary: A new trail in the national park traces the legacy of Welsh industry, while offering some of the UK’s finest riverside and mountain walks. The vital moment comes a couple of hours into the walk. I drop down from a tussocky hill towards the village of Y Fron.
body: This is the Llwybr Llechi Eryri (Snowdonia Slate Trail), an 83-mile hike that follows a great loop around the national park, starting in Bangor and ending in Bethesda. It strings together a series of abandoned slate quarries with some of the finest riverside and mountain walking in the UK. I’m doing just three days, starting in Llanberis and heading to Betws-y-Coed via stops in Beddgelert and Llan Ffestiniog.

Beyond Y Fron village, I descend into my first quarry, and it proves to be a classic. This was once the Dorothea slate quarry, a vast abandoned complex of railways, cottages and chasms. I start exploring: tunnels, cuttings, huge looming stone towers like Maya temples, all overgrown with ash, birch and oak. What strikes me is the craftsmanship and precision in construction, each stone hand-fitted without mortar, all for workaday industrial buildings.

highlights.title: Law Firm Linked to Elon Musk Started an ‘Election Integrity’ Organization
highlights.summary: The firm that helped set up Elon Musk’s America PAC is behind the new group, which will work with election officials to pursue policies aligned with Donald Trump’s false election fraud claims.
body: The law firm that helped set up Elon Musk’s America PAC has created a new, nationwide “election integrity” organization aligned with Donald Trump’s false claims of election fraud, WIRED has learned.

The organization, a nonprofit called the Association of State and Local Election Officials, was established by a lawyer then at Lex Politica, the Musk-linked law firm founded by Chris Gober, who was chief counsel for America PAC in 2024 and is now running in Texas for a spot in the House of Representatives.

The board of directors, according to the nonprofit’s registration filing in Texas, boasts Florida secretary of state Cord Byrd, current and former state election officials in Georgia, a Michigan state representative, and the president of Cleta Mitchell’s Election Integrity Network, a Trump administration-aligned election denial group. Byrd announced his involvement with the group—which he said won’t begin until after the election—alongside Florida governor Ron DeSantis in September, as the pair touted its mission, which aims to bring what they call “election integrity” policies down to the state and local level nationwide.

His initial reaction, to be fair, was mild: “The university’s Instagram account posted something talking a little trash about me last night, which I certainly love,” he said ahead of the Utes’ clash with the Houston Cougars last week.

Do you think we should be amplifying reasons for why people hate my guts as a university? I don’t know.”

highlights.title: I Put a Bunch of AI Agents in Charge of a Fantasy Soccer Team. They’re Not Better Than Humans—Yet
highlights.summary: To experiment with AI’s predictive skills, I let Codex loose on a fantasy team. It tried to bench Erling Haaland at first, but it soon learned the error of its ways.
body: I have consulted my AI-powered crystal ball, and it’s telling me that frontier models are going to get a lot better at making predictions in the near future. Just ask my Premier League fantasy team.

A few weeks ago, I deployed a small horde of AI agents to craft and manage an experimental roster. Given the proliferation of AI agents into pretty much every aspect of our lives, I wanted to know if a swarm of bots could put together a winning team.

I first looked at the potential for AI here a few years ago, playing around with a tool from the UK’s Turing Institute that selected teams after modeling previous fantasy league data. Its suggestions were remarkably bonkers—it didn’t incorporate real-world information, like a player’s injury or a team’s change in management.

This time, while on a flight to visit family, I asked Codex for help. First, I fed the model a couple of relevant research papers. Then, I asked it to build a harness—instructions and code that guides different agents through various steps—that would check recent news and run a model to make predictions.

highlights.title: Rachel Roddy’s pasta with Senegalese-inspired ragu – recipe
highlights.summary: A historical adventure deep in the very heart of pasta country in southern Italy unexpectedly unearths a sauce with roots in Senegal. About 30 kilometres south of Naples, the town of Gragnano is surrounded by the Monti Lattari mountain range – the limestone backbone of the Sorrento peninsula.
body: The natural slope of the terrain was fortuitous, because it allowed for the construction of a sequence of mills, which started in around 1263. During a visit to Gragnano last month, local historian Giuseppe Di Massa explained how it all worked; how gravity drove the flow of water from one mill to the next, in order to power vertical millstones – a system created for the inconsistent flow. The valley, with its clever water system, became known as the valley of the mills; its role milling grain, which arrived at the nearby port of Castellammare di Stabia, a vital operation to Naples and surrounding towns.

The activity of the 30 mills peaked during the 18th century, but another industry was growing, one that harnessed another natural aspect of the town: its climate. The temperature, humidity and sea breeze were ideal conditions for drying pasta.

highlights.title: GTA 6 Dog Poop Gameplay Premieres in the Latest Episode of South Park
highlights.summary: GTA 6 made a surprise appearance on South Park with just shy of 20 seconds of genuine, exclusive gameplay that showcased dog poop. The latest episode of Trey Parker and Matt Stone’s hit comedy series, titled Guinea Pig On A Stick, shows a dog doing a poo on a beach (this is South Park after all!).
body: The gameplay is shown during a scene in which the main characters visit a cattle ranche, where a woman hypes up GTA 6 by providing a quick look at the game. “The graphics are seriously next level,” the woman says. “You see the worldbuilding? It’s a dog taking a poop. And people can pick up the dog poop. You can throw things at the person with dog poop, and if they choose to fight back, you can pick up the dog poop and actually attack them with the dog poop. That is what’s coming in November.”
“Wow!” Stan says. “Holy s**t!” Kyle exclaims. “Dude, that game looks f***ing tits!” Cartman offers.

The woman is voiced by Tish Hicks (as confirmed in the credits of the episode). Hicks is a voice actor who narrated the GTA 5 gameplay trailer all those years ago, so fans will probably find her voice familiar.

As for the gameplay, Rockstar had confirmed the dog poop mechanic already, but it’s fun to see it in action. And it’s great to get a sense of the density of NPCs on the beach in gameplay, too, given this sort of scene has been at the heart of official pre-launch videos and screenshots.

highlights.summary: Out and about in New York City, Rosalía continues to expand her penchant for balletcore with outsized accessories and towering footwear.
body: Rosalía has a lot of baggage—and even more shoe. The Spanish pop star has never been one to do things by halves. Not when it comes to her music, and certainly not when it comes to fashion; especially not when it comes to accessories. Spotted out and about in New York City, the singer appeared to be carrying everything but the kitchen sink in an absolutely gargantuan leather bag, while teetering along in a pair of ballet shoes that took the humble flat to dizzying new heights. Traveling light? Not in Rosalía’s vocabulary.

Not content with an ordinary pair of ballet flats, Rosalía—who has been performing en pointe—opted for a pair of pale pink satin ballet platforms from Junko Shimada’s spring 2009 collection, with crisscrossing ankle ribbons, exaggerated black platforms, and transparent heels. The shoes have a fab pop cultural pedigree, too: Lady Gaga wore the shoes back in 2009, when her own penchant for architectural, gravity-defying footwear was in full swing. 15-plus years later, they look every bit as wonderfully impractical.
